summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style overview of Saudi Arabia. It describes the four historical regions that formed the area (Hejaz, Najd, Al-Ahsa and 'Asir) and how Ibn Saud united them into the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932 through conquests starting with Riyadh in 1902. It also covers the state's absolute monarchy, the influence of Wahhabism, the nickname 'Land of the Two Holy Mosques', and population figures for 2013 and 2017.
one_line: Overview of Saudi Arabia's history, unification under Ibn Saud, absolute monarchy, Wahhabi influence, holy sites and population.
key_facts: The area of modern-day Saudi Arabia formerly consisted of four distinct regions: Hejaz, Najd, parts of Eastern Arabia (Al-Ahsa) and Southern Arabia ('Asir).
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was founded in 1932 by Ibn Saud.
Ibn Saud united the four regions into a single state through a series of conquests beginning in 1902 with the capture of Riyadh.
Riyadh was the ancestral home of the House of Saud, Ibn Saud's family.
Saudi Arabia has since been an absolute monarchy, described in the note as effectively a hereditary dictatorship governed along Islamic lines.
The ultraconservative Wahhabi religious movement within Sunni Islam has been called 'the predominant feature of Saudi culture'.
The global spread of Wahhabism has been largely financed by the oil and gas trade.
Saudi Arabia is sometimes called 'the Land of the Two Holy Mosques'.
The name 'Land of the Two Holy Mosques' refers to Al-Masjid al-Haram in Mecca and Al-Masjid an-Nabawi in Medina.
Al-Masjid al-Haram and Al-Masjid an-Nabawi are described as the two holiest places in Islam.
As of 2013, Saudi Arabia had a total population of 28.7 million.
As of 2013, of the 28.7 million people, 20 million were Saudi nationals and 8 million were foreigners.
As of 2017, the population of Saudi Arabia is 33 million.
The state's official language is Arabic.
